cards.q: A spherical storage tank has a diameter of 12 m. What is the radius of the tank?
cards.why: The radius goes from the centre to the edge: half the diameter. 12 ÷ 2 = 6 m.
cards.hook: Diameter goes all the way across; radius is half of it.

cards.q: A spherical tank has radius 6 m. What is its volume, correct to the nearest m³?
cards.hook: Sphere volume: four-thirds pi r cubed. Cube the radius, not the diameter.

cards.q: Which formula gives the volume of a sphere of radius r?
cards.why: Volume is cubic, so r³: V = (4/3)πr³. 4πr² is the surface area and (2/3)πr³ is a hemisphere.
cards.hook: Volume has r³ (m³); area has r² (m²).

cards.q: A spherical tank has radius 6 m. What is its curved surface area, correct to one decimal place?
cards.why: Curved surface area of a sphere = 4πr² = 4π(6)² = 144π = 452.389… ≈ 452.4 m².
cards.hook: The skin of a sphere is four circles: 4πr².

cards.q: A tank has curved surface area 452.4 m² and volume 905 m³. One litre of paint covers 3.5 m². How many litres paint the curved surface, to the nearest litre?
cards.why: Paint covers the surface, so use the area: 452.4 ÷ 3.5 = 129.26… ≈ 129 litres.
cards.hook: Paint goes on the area, not the volume. "How many fit into" means divide.

cards.q: 129 litres of paint are needed. Paint is sold in 25 litre tins costing €180 each. What is the total cost of the paint?
cards.why: 129 ÷ 25 = 5.16, and you can’t buy part of a tin, so 6 tins: 6 × €180 = €1080.
cards.hook: Tins, boxes, buses: always round UP.

cards.q: A tank has a hemisphere at each end, each of radius 4.5 m. What is the volume of one hemispherical end, correct to the nearest m³?
cards.why: A hemisphere is half a sphere: V = (2/3)πr³ = (2/3)π(4.5)³ = 190.85… ≈ 191 m³.
cards.hook: Hemi = half: half of (4/3)πr³ is (2/3)πr³.

cards.q: A tank of volume 905 m³ is a cylinder of length h with a hemisphere (191 m³ each) at each end, all of radius 4.5 m. Which equation finds h?
cards.why: Parts add up to the total: two hemispheres plus the cylinder’s volume πr²h equals 905.
cards.hook: Write "parts = total" first, then solve for the one letter left.

cards.q: A tank of volume 905 m³ is a cylinder of length h m with a 191 m³ hemisphere at each end, all of radius 4.5 m. Find h, correct to one decimal place.
cards.hook: Take away both ends before dividing by πr².

cards.q: A billion is a thousand million. Write 165 billion in the form a × 10ⁿ, where 1 ≤ a < 10.
cards.hook: Multiplying powers of 10? Add the indices.

cards.q: Each sphere of the Atomium has a diameter of 18 metres. What is the radius of each sphere?
cards.why: The radius is half the diameter: 18 ÷ 2 = 9 m.
cards.hook: Radius = diameter ÷ 2. Halve it before any formula.

cards.q: Each sphere of the Atomium has radius 9 m. What is the volume of one sphere, correct to 2 decimal places?
cards.hook: Four-thirds pi r cubed: cube first, then × 4 ÷ 3 × π.

cards.q: The Atomium has 9 identical spheres, each of radius 9 m. What is the combined surface area of the 9 spheres, to the nearest m²?
cards.why: One sphere: 4πr² = 4π(9)² = 324π. Nine spheres: 9 × 324π = 2916π = 9160.88… ≈ 9161 m².
cards.hook: Find one, then multiply by how many there are.

cards.q: Which formula gives the curved surface area of a cylinder of radius r and height (length) h?
cards.why: Unrolled, the curved surface is a rectangle: the circumference 2πr by the height h, so 2πrh. πr²h is the volume.
cards.hook: Peel the label off a can: a rectangle 2πr wide and h tall.

cards.q: Each of 8 cylindrical pipes has radius 1.65 m and length 23 m. What is the sum of the curved surface areas of all 8 pipes, to the nearest m²?
cards.hook: Curved only: no circular ends. Then × 8 for 8 pipes.

cards.q: 12 equal cylindrical pipes, each of radius 1.45 m, have total curved surface area 3170 m². Which equation gives the length h of one pipe?
cards.why: One pipe has curved area 2πrh = 2π(1.45)h, and 12 of them make 3170 m².
cards.hook: Area of one × number of pipes = total area.

cards.q: 12 equal cylindrical pipes, each of radius 1.45 m, have total curved surface area 3170 m². Find the length of one pipe, to the nearest metre.
cards.hook: Share the total out first: ÷ 12 gives one pipe.

cards.q: Curved areas: 8 pipes 1908 m², 12 pipes 3170 m², 9 spheres 9161 m². Steel costs €70 per m². What is the cost of steel to cover all of them?
cards.hook: Total area first, then × the price per m².

cards.q: A field is cut into 8 strips of width 3 m. The heights are 4, 5.8, 7, 6.5, 6, 4.8, 6, 6.5 and 8 m. Use the trapezoidal rule to estimate its area.
cards.hook: h over 2, times: first + last + twice the rest.

cards.q: In the trapezoidal rule, which of the heights get doubled?
cards.right: All except the first and last
cards.why: Area ≈ (h/2)[first + last + 2(all the others)]: each middle height is shared by two strips, so it counts twice.
cards.hook: Ends once, middles twice: the middles are shared by two strips.

cards.q: Strips of width 4 m, heights 4, 6.4, 6.9, 6, x, 6.2, 8 m (the known middle heights add to 25.5). The trapezoidal area is 145.6 m². Which equation finds x?
cards.why: h/2 = 4/2 = 2; first + last = 4 + 8 = 12; x is a middle height, so it is doubled with the others.
cards.hook: An unknown height goes in the same place a number would.

cards.q: Strips of width 4 m, heights 4, 6.4, 6.9, 6, x, 6.2, 8 m. The trapezoidal rule gives the area as 145.6 m². What is x?
cards.hook: Multiply out the brackets carefully: 2 × 2x = 4x.

cards.q: You are constructing triangle ABC with |AB| = 8 cm, |AC| = 5 cm, |BC| = 7 cm. You have drawn [AB]. What next?
cards.right: Arcs: 5 cm from A, 7 cm from B
wrong: Arcs: 7 cm from A, 5 cm from B
A 90° angle at A, then 5 cm up
Arcs of 5 cm and 7 cm, both from A
cards.why: C is 5 cm from A and 7 cm from B, so draw those two arcs; where they cross is C. Leave the arcs showing.
cards.hook: Three sides given? Ruler for one, compass arcs for the other two.

cards.q: A square has side length 2k cm. What is its area, in terms of k?
cards.why: Area = side × side = (2k)(2k) = 4k²: square the 2 as well as the k.
cards.hook: (2k)² means 2k × 2k: square the number too.

cards.q: A right-angled isosceles triangle with two sides of 20 cm has a hypotenuse of 2k cm. Find k, correct to 2 decimal places.
cards.why: Pythagoras: (2k)² = 20² + 20², so 4k² = 800, k² = 200 and k = √200 = 14.14.
cards.hook: Pythagoras: hyp² = a² + b². Square the WHOLE 2k.

cards.q: A square of area 800 cm² has a right-angled triangle with two 20 cm sides cut from one corner. What is the area of the shaded part left?
cards.why: Triangle = ½ × 20 × 20 = 200 cm². Shaded part = square − triangle = 800 − 200 = 600 cm².
cards.hook: Shaded = whole − the bit cut out.

cards.q: The height of a cone equals the diameter of its base. The radius of the base is 2.25 m. What is the height of the cone?
cards.why: The diameter is twice the radius: 2 × 2.25 = 4.5 m, and the height equals the diameter.
cards.hook: Diameter = 2 × radius.

cards.q: A cone has vertical height 4.5 m and base radius 2.25 m. Which calculation gives its slant height l?
cards.why: Height, radius and slant height make a right-angled triangle with l the hypotenuse: l² = 4.5² + 2.25², l = 5.03 m.
cards.hook: Slant height is the hypotenuse: l² = h² + r².

cards.q: Which formula gives the curved surface area of a cone of base radius r?
cards.right: πrl, with l the slant height
wrong: πrh, with h the vertical height
cards.why: Curved surface area of a cone = πrl, using the slant height l. Adding πr² gives the total (with the base); (1/3)πr²h is the volume.
cards.hook: Curved surface: slant height. Volume: vertical height.
keys: πrl, using the slant height l

cards.q: A sculpture is 14 identical cones, each with base radius 2.25 m, height 4.5 m and slant height 5.03 m. What is their total curved surface area, to 2 decimal places?
cards.why: One cone: πrl = π(2.25)(5.03) = 35.55… m². Fourteen cones: 14 × 35.55… = 497.77 m².
cards.hook: Cone skin: πrl, with the slant height l.

cards.q: A sculpture has curved surface area 497.77 m². One litre of polish covers 12.25 m². How many litres are needed, to the nearest litre?
cards.why: 497.77 ÷ 12.25 = 40.63…, which is 41 litres to the nearest litre.
cards.hook: Coverage: area ÷ (m² per litre).

cards.q: 41 litres of polish are needed. A 5 litre container costs 110 Australian dollars (AUD), and AUD 1 = €0.68. What is the cost of the polish, to the nearest euro?
cards.hook: Round containers UP; to change AUD to €, multiply by the rate.

cards.q: The net of a cone’s curved surface is a sector. When the net is rolled up into the cone, the arc of the sector becomes…
cards.why: The arc wraps once round the bottom of the cone, so the arc length is the circumference of the base: p = 2πr.
cards.hook: Roll the sector up: its arc runs round the base.

cards.q: A cone has base radius 2.25 m and slant height 5.03 m. Its net is a sector of radius 5.03 m. Find the arc length p of the sector, to 2 decimal places.
cards.why: The arc wraps round the base of the cone, so p = 2πr = 2π(2.25) = 14.137… ≈ 14.14 m.
cards.hook: Arc of the net = circumference of the cone’s base.

cards.q: A sector of radius 5.03 m has arc length 14.14 m. Find θ, the angle at the centre, to the nearest degree.
cards.hook: Arc = (θ/360) × 2πr: the slice of the whole circumference.

cards.q: Square ABCD has sides of 7 cm. Tilted square PQRS has its corners on the sides of ABCD, with Q on [AB] and |AQ| = 5 cm. What is the area of PQRS?
cards.why: Each corner triangle has sides 5 and 2, area ½(5)(2) = 5. PQRS = 49 − 4(5) = 29 cm². (Or |PQ|² = 5² + 2² = 29.)
cards.hook: Tilted square = big square − 4 corner triangles.

cards.q: Square ABCD has sides of 7 cm; Q on [AB] with |AQ| = 5 cm, so the corner triangle has sides 5 cm and 2 cm. What is the side |PQ| of the tilted square?
cards.why: |PQ| is the hypotenuse of the corner triangle: |PQ|² = 5² + 2² = 29, so |PQ| = √29 cm.
cards.hook: Hypotenuse² = sum of the squares of the other two sides.

cards.q: Wheel u has radius 4 cm and wheel v has radius 6 cm. What are their circumferences, in terms of π?
cards.why: Circumference = 2πr: u = 2π(4) = 8π cm and v = 2π(6) = 12π cm.
cards.hook: Circumference 2πr (a length, cm); area πr² (cm²).

cards.q: Two wheels are in non-slip contact, so turning one turns the other. What is the same for both wheels?
cards.right: The distance moved by each rim
cards.why: The rims grip each other, so each moves the same distance. A smaller wheel has a shorter circumference, so it turns more times.
cards.hook: Non-slip: same rim distance, so the small wheel spins more.

cards.q: Wheel u (circumference 8π cm) and wheel v (circumference 12π cm) are in non-slip contact. Wheel v makes 100 rotations. How many rotations does u make?
cards.why: v’s rim moves 100 × 12π = 1200π cm. u’s rim moves the same, so u turns 1200π ÷ 8π = 150 times.
cards.hook: Distance ÷ circumference = number of turns.

cards.q: What is the volume of a solid sphere of radius 0.3 cm, in cm³, correct to 3 decimal places?
cards.hook: Sphere: (4/3)πr³. Cube small decimals carefully: 0.3³ = 0.027.

cards.q: A gold sphere has volume 0.113 cm³. Each cm³ of gold weighs 19.3 g. How many grams of gold are in the sphere, to 2 decimal places?
cards.why: Every cm³ weighs 19.3 g, so multiply: 0.113 × 19.3 = 2.1809 ≈ 2.18 g. (Rounding 0.113 to 0.11 first gives 2.12.)
cards.hook: Grams per cm³ × cm³ = grams. Round only at the end.

cards.q: There are about 6.02 × 10²³ atoms in 197 g of gold. How many atoms are in 2.18 g of gold? (a to 2 significant figures)
cards.hook: Go through 1: divide to get one gram, then multiply up.

cards.q: A random sample of 1560 television viewers was surveyed. What is the margin of error of the survey, as a percentage to 1 decimal place?
cards.hook: Margin of error: one over root n.

cards.q: In a survey of 1560 viewers (margin of error 2.5%), 546 said they liked the show. What is the 95% confidence interval for the percentage who like it?
cards.why: Sample proportion: 546 ÷ 1560 = 0.35 = 35%. Go 2.5% either side: 35 − 2.5 to 35 + 2.5, so 32.5% to 37.5%.
cards.hook: Confidence interval: sample % ± margin of error.

cards.q: An executive claims 40% of viewers like a show. A survey found 35% liked it. To test the claim, what is the null hypothesis?
cards.why: The null hypothesis is the claim being tested: H₀: p = 40%. The alternative is H₁: p ≠ 40%.
cards.hook: H₀ is the claim (an "equals"); H₁ says it is wrong.

cards.q: H₀: 40% of viewers like a show. The 95% confidence interval from a survey is 32.5% to 37.5%. What is the conclusion at the 5% level?
cards.right: Reject H₀: 40% is outside the interval
wrong: Don’t reject H₀: 40% is outside it
Don’t reject H₀: 35% is inside it
cards.why: 40% is not in [32.5%, 37.5%], so reject H₀: the evidence suggests the percentage who like the show is not 40%.
cards.hook: Claim inside the interval: keep it. Outside: reject it.

cards.q: A scale diagram (1 cm = 3 m) of a lawn is cut into 8 strips each 1 cm wide. Heights: 0, 5, 6, 5, 4, 5, 6, 5, 0 cm. Use the trapezoidal rule to estimate the real area.
cards.hook: Change every length to real metres first, then use the rule.

cards.q: On a scale diagram, 1 cm = 3 m. Each grid box is 0.5 cm tall. A vertical line is 10 boxes tall. What real length does it show?
cards.why: 10 boxes × 0.5 cm = 5 cm on the diagram, and each cm is 3 m, so 5 × 3 = 15 m.
cards.hook: Boxes → cm → metres: one step at a time.

cards.q: Nuala walks at a speed of 1.6 metres per second. What is this speed in kilometres per hour?
cards.why: In an hour (3600 s) she walks 1.6 × 3600 = 5760 m, and 5760 ÷ 1000 = 5.76 km. So 5.76 km/h.
cards.hook: m/s to km/h: × 3600 ÷ 1000, which is × 3.6.

cards.q: A crescent is made by removing a disc of radius 2.5 cm from a disc of radius 3 cm. What is the area of the crescent, to 2 decimal places?
cards.why: Area = big disc − small disc = π(3)² − π(2.5)² = 9π − 6.25π = 2.75π = 8.639… ≈ 8.64 cm².
cards.hook: Shape with a hole: area of the whole − area of the hole.

cards.q: A crescent is made by removing a disc of radius 2.5 cm from a disc of radius 3 cm. What is the perimeter of the crescent, to 2 decimal places?
cards.why: The edge runs round the outer circle and back round the inner one, so add: 2π(3) + 2π(2.5) = 11π = 34.557… ≈ 34.56 cm.
cards.hook: Perimeter: trace the whole edge. Both curves count, so add them.

cards.q: An inverted cone has vertical height 12 cm and radius 7 cm. What is its volume, to 2 decimal places?
cards.hook: A cone is one third of the cylinder around it: (1/3)πr²h.

cards.q: A cone of volume 615.75 cm³ is filled by a pipe at 0.5 litres per minute (1 litre = 1000 cm³). How long does it take, to the nearest second?
cards.why: 0.5 litres = 500 cm³ a minute. 615.75 ÷ 500 = 1.2315 minutes, and 1.2315 × 60 = 73.89 ≈ 74 seconds.
cards.hook: Litres → cm³: × 1000. Decimal minutes → seconds: × 60.

cards.q: What is the volume of a solid sphere of radius 3 cm, in terms of π?
cards.hook: “In terms of π”: work out the number, leave π as it is.

cards.q: A sphere of volume 36π cm³ is taken out of a full cylinder of water with internal radius 5 cm. Which equation gives the drop h in the water level?
cards.why: The lost water is a short cylinder of radius 5 and height h, with the same volume as the sphere: π(5)²h = 36π.
cards.hook: Volume out = volume of the sphere. The water is a cylinder: πr²h.

cards.q: A sphere of volume 36π cm³ is taken out of a full cylinder of water with internal radius 5 cm. By how much does the water level drop?
cards.why: π(5)²h = 36π, so 25πh = 36π and h = 36π ÷ 25π = 36 ÷ 25 = 1.44 cm (the π’s cancel).
cards.hook: Divide by the whole πr² — the π’s cancel.

cards.q: A cylinder has radius 5 cm and height 18 cm. Its curved surface is cut from a 35 cm by 20 cm sheet of metal. How much metal is left over, to 1 decimal place?
cards.why: Curved surface = 2πrh = 2π(5)(18) = 180π = 565.49 cm². Sheet = 35 × 20 = 700 cm². Left over = 700 − 565.49 ≈ 134.5 cm².
cards.hook: Left over = whole sheet − the piece cut out.

cards.q: A class surveyed a random sample of 800 people. What is the margin of error of the survey, as a percentage to 2 decimal places?
cards.hook: Margin of error = 1 ÷ √(sample size).

cards.q: In a random sample of 800 people (margin of error 3.54%), 350 supported a proposal. What is the 95% confidence interval for the percentage who support it?
cards.hook: Centre on the sample %, then go the margin of error each way.

cards.q: A newspaper claims 50% support a proposal. A survey gives a 95% confidence interval of 40.21% to 47.29%. What do you conclude at the 5% level?
cards.right: Reject the claim: 50% is outside it
wrong: Don’t reject: 50% is within 3.54% of it
cards.why: H₀: support is 50%. 50% is not in 40.21% to 47.29%, so reject H₀: support in the area is not 50%.
cards.hook: Test the CLAIM against the interval: outside means reject.

cards.q: A can’s net is cut from a sheet 16 cm tall: the side is a 10 cm tall rectangle, with the circular top (radius r) standing on it. What is r?
cards.why: The sheet’s height is 10 + one diameter = 16, so the diameter is 6 cm and the radius r = 6 ÷ 2 = 3 cm.
cards.hook: A circle stands one diameter tall: halve it for the radius.

cards.q: A can of radius 3 cm is made from a net. Its side is a rectangle of length y that wraps once round the can. Find y, to the nearest cm.
cards.why: The side wraps once round the circle, so y is the circumference: y = 2πr = 2π(3) = 6π = 18.85… ≈ 19 cm.
cards.hook: Wrap the side round the lid: its length = circumference 2πr.

cards.q: A 6π cm by 16 cm sheet gives a can’s side (6π by 10 cm) and its top and bottom (circles of radius 3 cm). What area is wasted, to the nearest cm²?
cards.why: Sheet 96π − side 60π − two circles 2π(3)² = 18π. Waste = 96π − 78π = 18π = 56.55 ≈ 57 cm².
cards.hook: Waste = sheet − every piece used (side, top AND bottom).

cards.q: What is the volume of a spherical ice cube of radius 1.5 cm, in terms of π?
cards.hook: Sphere: (4/3)πr³. Cube first: 1.5³ = 3.375.

cards.q: Ice cubes are held fully under the water in a cylinder, and the level rises by h. The volume of the risen layer of water (a cylinder of height h) equals…
cards.right: the volume of all the ice cubes
wrong: the volume of one ice cube
the surface area of the ice cubes
cards.why: The ice pushes up exactly its own volume of water, so π(3.5)²h = the total volume of the ice cubes put in.
cards.hook: Volume in = volume of the rise.

cards.q: Three ice spheres, each 4.5π cm³, are fully submerged in a cylinder of water of internal radius 3.5 cm. Find the rise h in the water level, to 1 decimal place.
cards.hook: Count every sphere, then divide by r² (the π’s cancel).

cards.q: Across a lake, every 10 m along [PQ], the offsets above + below the line are: 0+10, 20+20, 10+20, 30+20, 30+10, 20+20, 0. Estimate the lake’s area (trapezoidal rule).
cards.hook: Add the offsets above and below first: that is the width.

cards.q: A lake has a surface area of 2050 m² and is, on average, 8 m deep. Estimate the volume of water in the lake.
cards.why: Treat the lake as a slab: area × average depth = 2050 × 8 = 16 400 m³. The average depth already allows for the sloping bed.
cards.hook: Volume of a slab = area of the top × depth.

cards.q: What is the volume of a hemisphere of radius 21 cm, in terms of π?
cards.hook: Hemisphere = half a sphere: (2/3)πr³.

cards.q: A buoy is a cone standing on a hemisphere, both of radius 21 cm. The total height of the buoy is the height of the cone plus…
wrong: the slant height of the cone
cards.why: The hemisphere hangs below the cone, and its depth is its radius, 21 cm. So total height = cone height + 21.
cards.hook: A hemisphere is as deep as its radius.

cards.q: A buoy is a cone on a hemisphere, both radius 21 cm. The cone’s volume equals the hemisphere’s, 6174π cm³. What is the total height of the buoy?
cards.why: (1/3)π(21)²h = 6174π, so 147h = 6174 and the cone’s height is 42 cm. Add the hemisphere’s depth: 42 + 21 = 63 cm.
cards.hook: Solve for the cone’s height, then add the hemisphere’s radius.

cards.q: In triangle PBQ, |PB| = 43 m, |BQ| = 26 m and |PQ| = 60 m. Which rule finds the angle QBP?
cards.why: All three sides are known and no angle, so use the cosine rule: 60² = 26² + 43² − 2(26)(43)cos B.
cards.hook: Three sides, no angle? Cosine rule.

cards.q: In triangle PBQ, |PB| = 43 m, |BQ| = 26 m and |PQ| = 60 m. Find the angle QBP, correct to two decimal places.
cards.hook: Angle opposite the longest side; a minus cos means over 90°.

cards.q: The top of a lighthouse is a hemisphere of radius 3 m. What is the volume of the hemisphere, in terms of π?
cards.hook: Hemisphere: half of (4/3)πr³ is (2/3)πr³.

cards.q: A cylinder of radius 3 m has volume 36π m³. What is its height h?
cards.why: πr²h = 36π, so π(3)²h = 36π, 9πh = 36π and h = 36π ÷ 9π = 4 m.
cards.hook: Volume ÷ (area of the circular end) = height.

cards.q: A cone has base radius 7.5 m and vertical height 47 m. Find the angle A between its slanting side and its base, to the nearest degree.
cards.why: Cut the cone in half: a right-angled triangle with 47 opposite A and 7.5 next to it. tan A = 47 ÷ 7.5, so A = 80.93… ≈ 81°.
cards.hook: Height is opposite the base angle; the radius is adjacent. TOA.

cards.q: A cone of radius 7.5 m and height 47 m has its top cut off at a level circle of radius 3 m. What is the height k of the part left?
cards.why: The removed top is a similar cone: x/47 = 3/7.5, so x = 18.8 m. What is left: k = 47 − 18.8 = 28.2 m.
cards.hook: Similar cones: match radius to radius and height to height.

cards.q: A lighthouse can be seen from anywhere within a circle of radius 50 km. What is the area of the circle, to the nearest km²?
cards.hook: Area of a circle: πr². 2πr is the distance round it.

cards.q: 50 km = 27 nautical miles. How many km are in 1 nautical mile, correct to 4 significant figures?
cards.why: 27 nautical miles = 50 km, so 1 nautical mile = 50 ÷ 27 = 1.85185… ≈ 1.852 km (the 5th figure, 8, rounds the 1 up).
cards.hook: Unitary method: divide to get ONE, then multiply.

cards.q: The top of a lighthouse is 49 m above sea level. From a ship, its angle of elevation is 1.2°. Which equation gives the horizontal distance d?
cards.why: The 49 m height is opposite the 1.2° angle and d is adjacent to it, so tan 1.2° = 49/d.
cards.hook: Opposite and adjacent? Tan (TOA).

cards.q: The top of a lighthouse is 49 m above sea level. From a ship, its angle of elevation is 1.2°. Find the horizontal distance d, in km to 2 decimal places.
cards.why: d = 49 ÷ tan 1.2° = 2339.2… m, and ÷ 1000 gives 2.34 km. (Calculator in degree mode.)
cards.hook: Metres to km: ÷ 1000. Check DEG mode on the calculator.

cards.q: A shed is 8.5 m high at its highest point. Which is most likely true, with a height for Seán to back it up?
cards.right: 5 times as high: Seán about 1.7 m
wrong: 3 times as high: Seán about 2.8 m
8 times as high: Seán about 1.1 m
5 times as high: Seán about 42.5 m
cards.why: Divide the shed’s height by each number: 8.5 ÷ 5 = 1.7 m, a normal adult height. 8.5 ÷ 3 = 2.8 m is too tall; 8.5 ÷ 8 = 1.06 m is a small child.
cards.hook: Test each claim: divide, then ask "is that a real person?"

cards.q: A shed is a prism 18 m long. Its front is a 12 m wide, 7 m high rectangle with a triangular roof on top, 8.5 m high at its peak. What is its volume?
cards.why: Front = rectangle 12 × 7 = 84 + triangle ½(12)(1.5) = 9, so 93 m². Volume = 93 × 18 = 1674 m³.
cards.hook: Prism: area of the front face × length. Roof height = 8.5 − 7.

cards.q: A shed has a volume of 1674 m³, and 1 m³ = 1000 litres. What is its capacity in litres?
cards.why: Each m³ holds 1000 litres, so multiply: 1674 × 1000 = 1 674 000 litres, which is over one million.
cards.hook: m³ to litres: × 1000 (a cubic metre is a big box).

cards.q: A roof is 12 m wide and rises from 7 m to 8.5 m, with its peak above the centre. Find its slant length d, to 1 decimal place.
cards.why: Half the roof is a right-angled triangle: across 12 ÷ 2 = 6, up 8.5 − 7 = 1.5. d² = 6² + 1.5² = 38.25, so d = 6.18… ≈ 6.2 m.
cards.hook: Draw the right-angled triangle first: half the width, the rise.

cards.q: To enlarge a shape with centre A and scale factor 3, you draw a ray from A through each corner. Where does each image corner go?
cards.right: On the ray, 3 times as far from A
wrong: On the ray, 3 cm further out
On the ray, ⅓ as far from A
On the ray, 4 times as far from A
cards.why: Scale factor 3: measure from A to the corner, multiply by 3, and mark the image point that far from A on the same ray.
cards.hook: Always measure from the centre of enlargement.

cards.q: In triangle ABC, |AB| = 3 m, |AC| = 7 m and the angle at A is 30°. Which gives |BC|²?
cards.why: Two sides and the angle between them: cosine rule. |BC|² = 3² + 7² − 2(3)(7)cos 30° = 21.627, so |BC| = 4.65 m.
cards.hook: Two sides and the angle between: cosine rule (it isn’t right-angled).
keys: Two sides and the angle between them

cards.q: In triangle ABC, |AB| = 3 m, |AC| = 7 m, |BC| = 4.65 m and the angle at A is 30°. Find the angle ACB, to the nearest degree.
cards.why: Angle C is opposite the 3 m side: sin C / 3 = sin 30° / 4.65, so sin C = 0.3225… and C = 18.8… ≈ 19°.
cards.hook: Sine rule: pair each angle with the side opposite it.

cards.q: A rectangular garden measures 50 m by 30 m. What is the area of the whole garden?
cards.why: Area of a rectangle = length × width = 50 × 30 = 1500 m².
cards.hook: Area: multiply. Perimeter: add all the way round.

cards.q: A pond is 18 m long. Its widths every 3 m are 0, 10, 14, 12, 10, 8 and 2 m. Use the trapezoidal rule to estimate the area of the pond.
cards.hook: h/2 × [first + last + 2 × (all the middle ones)].

cards.q: How could the trapezoidal rule (with different measurements) give a more accurate estimate of the area of a pond?
cards.right: Measure the widths at smaller intervals
wrong: Measure the widths at larger intervals
Double the first and last widths too
Round each width to the nearest 5 m
cards.why: Each strip is treated as a straight-sided trapezium. Thinner strips (more measurements) follow the curved edge more closely.
cards.hook: More, thinner strips hug the curve better.

cards.q: A 1500 m² garden has a pond of actual area 172 m² (estimated 165 m²). The rest is grass, resown at €2.55 per m². What is the cost, to the nearest ten euro?
cards.why: Grass = 1500 − 172 = 1328 m² (use the actual area). 1328 × 2.55 = €3386.40, which is €3390 to the nearest ten euro.
cards.hook: Grass = garden − pond. Nearest ten: look at the units digit.

cards.q: Materials cost £840, which includes an import duty of 16.9%. £840 is what percentage of the price before duty?
cards.why: The price before duty is 100%. Adding 16.9% duty makes it 116.9%, so £840 = 116.9%.
cards.hook: Price with the tax added = 100% + the tax %.

cards.q: Materials cost £840, which includes an import duty of 16.9%. What was the cost before the duty was added, to the nearest penny?
cards.hook: Going back: divide by 1.169. Don’t take 16.9% off £840.

cards.q: A bill of £840 is paid in euro, at €1 = £0.8547, plus a commission of 2.5% of the £840. What is the total paid in euro, to the nearest cent?
cards.hook: €1 = £0.8547: pounds to euro, divide by 0.8547.

cards.q: A square has sides of 12 cm. Circle c is inside the square and touches all four sides. What is the radius of c?
cards.why: c touches opposite sides, so its diameter is the side of the square, 12 cm. Radius = 12 ÷ 2 = 6 cm.
cards.hook: A circle that fits snugly in a square: diameter = side.
keys: its diameter is the side of the square

cards.q: A circle has radius 6 cm. What is its area, correct to 2 decimal places?
cards.hook: Area πr² (square the radius); 2πr is the circumference.

cards.q: A circle of area 113.10 cm² fits inside a square of side 12 cm. What percentage of the square’s area does the circle take up, to the nearest percent?
cards.hook: Percentage = part ÷ whole × 100. The whole goes underneath.

cards.q: Circle k goes through the four corners of a square of side 12 cm, and has the same centre. Which calculation gives the radius of k?
cards.why: Centre to corner: across 6 and up 6, so r² = 6² + 6² = 72 and r = √72 = 8.49 cm. √(12² + 12²) is the whole diagonal (the diameter).
cards.hook: Radius = half the diagonal: centre to corner.

cards.q: Circle k has radius 8.49 cm. What is its circumference, correct to 2 decimal places?
cards.why: Circumference = 2πr = 2π(8.49) = 53.344… ≈ 53.34 cm.
cards.hook: Circumference: 2πr, or πd. Not both 2 and d!

cards.q: A cylindrical paddling pool has internal diameter 2.4 m and depth 0.9 m. It is filled to a depth of 0.75 m. What is the volume of water, to 2 decimal places?
cards.hook: Halve the diameter, and use the depth of the WATER.

cards.q: Each of 3 pool seats is a cube with sides of 0.5 m. What is the total volume of the 3 seats?
cards.hook: Cube volume = side³. A decimal cubed gets smaller.

cards.q: A cylindrical pool of radius 1.2 m holds water 0.6 m deep. Seats of total volume 0.375 m³ go fully under water. By how much does the level rise, to 2 decimal places?
cards.why: The rise is a cylinder with the seats’ volume: π(1.2)²h = 0.375, so h = 0.375 ÷ 4.524 = 0.0829 ≈ 0.08 m.
cards.hook: Rise × πr² = volume put in. The rise, not the new depth.

cards.q: A cone-shaped cover has radius 1.3 m and vertical height 0.8 m. What is its slant height l, to 2 decimal places?
cards.hook: Slant height is the hypotenuse: square, add, square root.

cards.q: A cone-shaped cover has radius 1.3 m, vertical height 0.8 m and slant height 1.53 m. What is its curved surface area, to 2 decimal places?
cards.why: Curved surface area = πrl = π(1.3)(1.53) = 6.2486… ≈ 6.25 m². It uses the slant height, not 0.8.
cards.hook: Cone skin: πrl. No base: it is a cover.

cards.q: A cone (radius 1.3 m, height 0.8 m, slant height 1.53 m) is cut open and laid flat: a sector of radius x. What is x?
cards.why: The sector’s radius runs from the tip of the cone down its side to the base, so x is the slant height: 1.53 m.
cards.hook: In the net, the slant height becomes the sector’s radius.

cards.q: A cone of base radius 1.3 m opens out into a sector of radius 1.53 m. Find the sector’s angle A, to the nearest degree.
cards.hook: Arc of the sector = circumference of the base.

cards.q: The fastest women’s serve at Wimbledon 2023 was 121 miles per hour. Using 1 mile = 1.61 km, how many km is 121 miles?
cards.why: Each mile is 1.61 km, so 121 miles = 121 × 1.61 = 194.81 km. (A km is shorter than a mile, so there are more of them.)
cards.hook: Miles to km: × 1.61 — the km number is always bigger.

cards.q: How many seconds are in one hour?
cards.why: An hour has 60 minutes and each minute has 60 seconds: 60 × 60 = 3600 seconds.
cards.hook: Time is in 60s, not 100s: 60 × 60 = 3600.

cards.q: A serve travels at 194.81 km per hour, and 1 hour = 3600 seconds. What is this speed in metres per second, to 2 decimal places?
cards.hook: km/h to m/s: × 1000 for metres, ÷ 3600 for seconds.

cards.q: The smallest tennis ball allowed has a radius of 3.27 cm. What is its surface area, to 2 decimal places?
cards.why: Surface area of a sphere = 4πr² = 4π(3.27)² = 134.3709… ≈ 134.37 cm².
cards.hook: Sphere skin: 4πr² (squared, cm²). Volume is (4/3)πr³.

cards.q: A tennis ball has external radius 3.4 cm; its air-filled centre has radius 3.1 cm. What is the volume of the rubber layer, to 2 decimal places?
cards.hook: A hollow shell: big volume − small volume, not (big − small)³.

cards.q: Three tennis balls of radius 3.4 cm are stacked one on top of the other in the smallest closed cylinder. What is the height h of the cylinder?
cards.why: Each ball is one diameter tall: 2 × 3.4 = 6.8 cm. Three balls: 3 × 6.8 = 20.4 cm (six radii).
cards.hook: Stacked balls: count diameters, not radii.

cards.q: A closed cylinder holds 3 tennis balls exactly: radius 3.4 cm, height 20.4 cm. What is the volume of the cylinder, to the nearest whole number?
cards.hook: Cylinder volume: πr²h, with the radius (half the width).

cards.q: Three tennis balls of radius 3.4 cm are stacked in the smallest closed rectangular box. What are the box’s dimensions?
cards.why: One ball must fit across, so the base is one diameter each way, 6.8 by 6.8; the height is three diameters, 20.4.
cards.hook: A ball needs a full diameter in every direction.
keys: the base is one diameter each way

cards.q: A closed rectangular box measures 6.8 cm × 6.8 cm × 20.4 cm. What is its total surface area?
cards.why: Two square ends 2(6.8 × 6.8) = 92.48 plus four sides 4(6.8 × 20.4) = 554.88: total 647.36 cm².
cards.hook: Closed box: six faces, in three matching pairs.
